title: Service continuity phrasing and incident scenarios
content:
Purpose:
This is a go-to-market working note that collects simple, customer-facing language and scenario-driven narratives we can reuse across sales collateral, status updates, and press responses. Focus: how Redwood talks about graceful degradation, multi-region fallbacks, and deterministic fallback behavior so customers feel informed and trust we’ll keep their apps available.

Audience:
- Sales & account execs preparing enterprise briefings
- Customer success and support for incident comms
- Product marketing for docs and website copy
- Engineers who want to align on customer-facing guarantees

Principles for trust language (one-liners we can reuse):
- Be specific: name the fallback (e.g., model variant, region) and the expected impact (latency or capability).
- Be proactive: communicate what we’ll do before customers see errors if we can (advance notice in console/console alerts).
- Emphasize continuity: highlight what remains available (tokens, embeddings, limited generation) rather than only what’s degraded.
- Frame choices: explain why a fallback helps (keeps the app online, preserves P95 latency, prevents queue build-up).
- Avoid false promises: don’t promise zero degradation; promise predictable degradation and clear SLAs for failover behavior.

Key fallback modalities (how to describe them succinctly):
- Model tier fallback: "When the selected high-performance variant exceeds capacity, Redwood automatically routes requests to a compatible, slightly lower-latency-optimized model variant that preserves output quality for most prompts."
- Region reroute: "If a region experiences capacity or network instability, requests are routed to the nearest healthy region with minimal IPST (in-path switch time) to keep latency stable."
- Capacity-tier fallback: "Traffic will temporarily shift from reserved Dedicated nodes to burst pools or hosted lanes to avoid throttling—this may increase per-token latency but keeps responses flowing."
- Degraded mode (limited features): "We can serve responses without rich tool-calling/structured streaming; developers receive plain-text generations while we recover advanced runtime features."

Scenario-driven messaging (templates + examples)
1) Minor degradation: transient latency spike (P95 rise)
- Status-line: "Minor latency spike in us-west-2 affecting generation P95. No request loss; most requests complete with higher latency. Engineers are actively rebalancing capacity."
- Customer email snippet: "We detected increased response times for a subset of requests in us-west-2. Our automatic routing adjusted traffic to healthy nodes — you may see slightly higher latencies for 5–10 minutes. No data loss. We’ll follow up when P95 is back to normal."

2) Targeted capacity shortage: Dedicated pool saturated
- Status-line: "Certain Dedicated pools are experiencing capacity saturation. We initiated the configured fallback to compatible hosted variants to preserve throughput; some long-running prompt sessions may reset."
- Customer email: "To keep your application responsive we routed traffic to a compatible hosted model variant. Most prompts will return comparable outputs; we flagged prompts that may hit advanced quantization differences. We’ll coordinate a post-incident report with token-level impact and compensation for any SLA breaches."

3) Multi-region outage with routing fallback
- Status-line: "Packet loss between regions caused elevated error rates for a portion of global traffic. Traffic was rerouted to secondary regions in real time; redundancy preserved request completion for 92% of impacted queries."
- Customer-facing press/enterprise line: "We automatically redirected traffic to secondary regions. For latency-sensitive workloads, P95 increased by ~20–30ms. Where regional data isolation was required, we honored retention rules and provided immediate next-step options with our account team."

4) Functional degradation (feature-limited fallback)
- Status-line: "Tool-calling and streaming temporarily suspended while the runtime recovers. Core generation remains available in non-streaming mode."
- Customer note: "We’ve temporarily disabled streaming and tool-calls to prioritize fresh requests; you’ll get full text responses but without real-time streaming. Our engineers expect to restore streaming within X hours; we’ll post updates every 30 minutes."

Sample short bullets for status page incidents (snappy, repeatable):
- "Impact: higher latency for some requests"
- "Scope: customers in region X and some cross-region traffic"
- "Action: automatic reroute to healthy nodes; Dedicated -> hosted fallback engaged"
- "Mitigation ETA: 30–90 minutes"

Sales & AE talking points (concise):
- "Redwood's fallback architecture is deterministic: you can map which variant or region will be used during a policy-triggered failover—no black box routing surprises."
- "We expose per-route fallback policies so you can choose strict regional isolation or availability-first routing depending on compliance needs."
- "We instrument and trace fallbacks end-to-end; you get token-level visibility and cost analytics for any routed requests so you can reconcile behavior post-incident."

Competitive differentiation to highlight (language for decks):
- "Predictable degradation: other vendors either throttle silently or return degraded outputs without clear versioning. Redwood’s fallback preserves model semantics and gives you a clear audit trail of which model variant served each request."
- "Policy-first routing: unlike basic multi-region stacks, our control plane lets you encode business intent (latency-first vs compliance-first) and we honor that during incidents."

Open questions / unresolved points to refine with product/engineering:
- How to quantify expected quality delta between model-tier fallbacks in customer-facing language without promising exact KL or ROUGE numbers? (engineering input needed)
- Default fallback policy wording in T&Cs / SLRs vs customizable language for enterprise contracts
- Standard compensation phrasing for SLA breaches linked to fallback activation

Quick templates (copy/paste)
- Status page: "[HH:MM UTC] Reduced performance in <region>. Automatic reroute engaged. No data loss reported. Engineers investigating. Updates every 30m."
- Customer email (short): "We routed some traffic from <region> to a fallback variant to preserve availability. Expect slightly different latency/behavior for up to <X> minutes. No customer data exposed. Contact <AE/email> for account-level details."
- Sales one-liner: "Redwood keeps your app online by routing to compatible model and region fallbacks while preserving output quality and auditability."

Next steps / owners:
- PM (Marta) to provide a one-paragraph approved wording for model-quality delta by 2026-03-10.
- SRE (Devon) to provide a matrix of fallback behaviors (latency, expected P95 delta) by region by 2026-03-15 so we can use numbers in sales materials.
- Comms (Priya) to convert templates into canned email snippets in Intercom and the status page by 2026-03-01.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a short "fallback explorer" in the Console that shows, for a given route, which variants/regions would be used at which thresholds (great sales/tech-demo tool).
- Keep the tone calm and engineering-forward: customers trust specifics and observability more than generic reassuring language.

End of doc. 
(Working draft — intended as reusable phrasing and scenario catalog; feel free to paste sections into intercom macros or AE playbooks.)
